subject: Science
title: Arjun's Cricket Adventure: Understanding Force and Pressure
hook: Why does a cricket ball hurt when it hits, but water doesn't? Learn force and pressure.

characters.name: Coach Vikram
characters.role: cricket coach who explains using sports

slides.title: Force and Pressure
slides.storyContext: Arjun is playing cricket on a sunny afternoon in Delhi when the ball hits his arm.

slides.title: The Cricket Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun gets hurt when the cricket ball hits him at 60 km/h, but when he falls into the swimming pool, the water (also moving) doesn't hurt at all. Why? Coach Vikram says it's about force and pressure, and Arjun sets out to understand.

slides.title: What is Force?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Force is a push or pull that can change the motion or shape of an object.

points.label: SI Unit
points.text: Newton (N), named after Isaac Newton.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Kicking a football, pulling a rope, a magnet attracting iron, gravity pulling you down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Force is anything that pushes or pulls something and makes it move or change shape.

slides.title: Types of Force: Contact and Non-Contact

points.label: Contact Forces
points.text: Forces where objects touch: friction, normal force, tension (like pulling a rope).

points.label: Non-Contact Forces
points.text: Forces that work without touching: gravity, magnetic force, electric force.

points.label: Daily Example
points.text: When Arjun catches the cricket ball, the ball and his hand touch—that's contact force.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some forces need things to touch; others work from a distance.

slides.title: What is Pressure?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Pressure = Force divided by Area. P = F/A

points.label: SI Unit
points.text: Pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: The SAME force spread over a larger area creates LESS pressure.

example.problem: A cricket ball (mass 160 g) hits Arjun's arm at 60 km/h. The contact area is 4 cm². Calculate the pressure if the impact force is 200 N.
example.solution: Area = 4 cm² = 4 × 10⁻⁴ m²; Pressure = F/A = 200 / (4 × 10⁻⁴) = 500,000 Pa = 5 × 10⁵ Pa. That's why it hurts!

slides.inSimpleWords: Pressure is force spread over an area. Sharp things hurt more because they concentrate force into a tiny area.

slides.title: Pressure in Liquids: Why Water Doesn't Hurt

points.label: Liquid Pressure
points.text: Pressure in a liquid depends on depth: P = ρgh (where ρ is density, g is gravity, h is depth).

points.label: Equal Pressure
points.text: Water pressure acts equally in all directions on a submerged object.

points.label: Why Water Feels Soft
points.text: The force is spread over Arjun's entire body, not concentrated on one spot—so pressure is lower even though water pushes from all sides.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water pushes on you from all sides at once, so pressure is spread out and doesn't hurt like a ball.

slides.title: Atmospheric Pressure: The Invisible Force

points.label: What It Is
points.text: The weight of air pushing down on everything at sea level: ~101,325 Pa.

points.label: Why We Don't Feel It
points.text: Pressure inside our body is equal to pressure outside, so they cancel out.

points.label: Indian Example
points.text: When a suction cup sticks to a bathroom tile in Mumbai, it's atmospheric pressure holding it—the air inside is thinner than outside.

slides.inSimpleWords: Air is always pushing on us, but we don't notice because pressure pushes equally from inside and outside.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Pressure from a Needle vs. a Finger

example.problem: A force of 50 N is applied to your skin. Using a needle (area = 0.5 mm² = 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ m²) vs. your fingertip (area = 1 cm² = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m²). Calculate pressure in each case.
example.solution: Needle pressure = 50 / (0.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 100,000,000 Pa = 10⁸ Pa (pierces skin). Finger pressure = 50 / (1 × 10⁻⁴) = 500,000 Pa = 5 × 10⁵ Pa (doesn't pierce). A needle hurts because pressure is concentrated!

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Better Bed
slides.storyContext: Priya's grandmother gets bedsores because pressure concentrates on her bones. Design a bed that spreads pressure better.

example.problem: A 60 kg person lies on a bed. Without support, all 60 × 10 = 600 N of force pushes on a small area (back, hips, heels). What should you do to reduce pressure?
example.solution: Add a mattress or foam to increase the contact area. If the mattress spreads the weight over 2 m², pressure = 600 / 2 = 300 Pa (much less). Memory foam works even better by conforming to the body.

slides.inSimpleWords: To reduce pressure on a person, increase the area the force is spread over—like a good mattress.

points.text: Force is a push or pull measured in Newtons (N).
Pressure = Force / Area, measured in Pascals (Pa).
Contact forces need objects to touch; non-contact forces work from a distance.
The same force spread over a larger area = less pressure (why wide shoes don't hurt as much as narrow heels).
Liquid pressure acts equally in all directions, which is why falling in water doesn't hurt like getting hit by a ball.
Atmospheric pressure pushes on everything, but we don't feel it because it pushes equally from inside and outside.

subject: Science
title: Kavi's Traffic Jam: The Science of Friction
hook: Why do cars need brakes? Why do you slip on wet floors? It's all about friction.

characters.name: Kavi
characters.role: young driver learning about his parents' car

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: Kavi's mother who uses friction every day

slides.title: Friction
slides.storyContext: Kavi is stuck in a Delhi traffic jam when his mother explains why cars need brakes.

slides.title: Why Can't We Stop?
slides.storyContext: Kavi watches a car slide on wet road during monsoon season and asks his mother why brakes don't work as well on wet roads. She says it's because of friction, and Kavi decides to understand this force that affects everything from his skateboard to his cricket shoes to the kitchen floor.

slides.title: What is Friction?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Friction is a force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact.

points.label: Direction
points.text: Friction always acts OPPOSITE to the direction of motion.

points.label: Cause
points.text: It happens because surfaces are not perfectly smooth—they have tiny bumps that catch each other.

slides.inSimpleWords: Friction is the force that tries to slow down or stop things from moving.

slides.title: Static vs. Kinetic Friction

points.label: Static Friction
points.text: Friction when an object is NOT moving. It keeps things in place (like a book on a tilted table).

points.label: Kinetic Friction
points.text: Friction when an object IS moving. It slows it down (like sliding a book across a table).

points.label: Comparison
points.text: Static friction is usually STRONGER than kinetic friction—that's why it's hard to START moving something, but easier to keep it moving.

example.problem: Kavi tries to push a heavy box across the garage floor. It takes 100 N of force to start it moving, but only 60 N to keep it moving. Why?
example.solution: Static friction (100 N) is greater than kinetic friction (60 N). Once the box starts moving, the bumps on the surfaces are less engaged, so less force is needed.

slides.inSimpleWords: It's harder to START moving something than to KEEP it moving.

slides.title: Friction Depends on Surface and Weight

points.label: Rough Surfaces
points.text: More friction between rough surfaces (sandpaper on wood) than smooth surfaces (ice on glass).

points.label: Weight Matters
points.text: Heavier objects have more friction (a truck is harder to push than a car).

points.label: Formula
points.text: Friction ≈ Coefficient of friction × Normal force (f = μN).

slides.inSimpleWords: Rough, heavy things have more friction. Smooth, light things have less.

slides.title: Friction in Daily Life: Good and Bad

points.label: Good Friction
points.text: Brakes in cars (friction stops the wheels), grip in shoes (friction keeps you from slipping), matches (friction creates heat and spark).

points.label: Bad Friction
points.text: Wears out car tires, makes machinery hot and inefficient, slows down runners.

points.label: Indian Example
points.text: Monsoon rains reduce friction between tires and roads, causing accidents. Dry weather = more grip = safer driving.

slides.inSimpleWords: Friction is a helper (stopping cars, gripping shoes) but also a problem (wearing out things, wasting energy).

slides.title: Reducing Friction: Lubrication and Smoothing

points.label: Lubrication
points.text: Oil and grease reduce friction between moving parts in engines, bicycle chains, and door hinges.

points.label: Polishing
points.text: Smoothing surfaces reduces friction (that's why ice skating works—ice is smooth).

points.label: Rollers and Bearings
points.text: Ball bearings reduce friction better than sliding surfaces by converting sliding to rolling.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use oil, make surfaces smooth, or use rollers to reduce friction.

example.problem: A car (mass 1000 kg) moving at 20 m/s brakes on a dry road. Coefficient of friction is 0.7, and on a wet road it's 0.4. Normal force = Weight = 1000 × 10 = 10,000 N. Calculate braking friction on each road.
example.solution: Dry: f = 0.7 × 10,000 = 7,000 N. Wet: f = 0.4 × 10,000 = 4,000 N. Wet roads have LESS friction, so braking distance is longer and accidents are more likely.

slides.title: Challenge: Why Do Cricket Players Wear Studs?
slides.storyContext: Kavi plays cricket and wears shoes with studs on the bottom. Meera asks why regular shoes don't work as well on wet grass.

example.problem: A cricket player wearing flat shoes (contact area 200 cm²) can barely stand on wet grass. With studs (total contact area 20 cm², but each stud digs in), friction increases. Explain why studs help even though the area is smaller.
example.solution: Studs dig into the grass and mud, increasing the effective roughness and creating more grip. The small, concentrated pressure (high pressure = deep penetration) from studs creates more friction than flat shoes can manage on slippery surfaces. Pressure helps friction when it grips into the surface.

slides.inSimpleWords: Studs dig into soft ground, creating better grip than flat shoes, even though studs touch less area.

points.text: Friction is a force that opposes motion and acts in the opposite direction.
Static friction (at rest) is stronger than kinetic friction (moving).
Friction depends on how rough the surfaces are and how heavy the object is.
Good friction: brakes, grip, matches. Bad friction: wear and tear, wasted energy.
Reduce friction with lubrication (oil), smoothing, or rollers.
Wet surfaces have less friction than dry surfaces, which is why roads are slippery in rain.

subject: Science
title: Dev's Diwali Discovery: The Mystery of Sound
hook: Why do firecrackers make noise? How does music travel from a speaker to your ear?

characters.name: Dev
characters.role: curious student fascinated by Diwali sounds

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Dev's cousin who plays the flute

slides.title: Sound
slides.storyContext: Dev is playing with crackers during Diwali when he notices something strange: the sound reaches him after the light, but they happen at the same place.

slides.title: The Diwali Mystery
slides.storyContext: During Diwali, Dev sees a distant firecracker explode. He notices the light reaches him immediately, but the sound takes a moment. Grandpa Hari explains that sound travels as waves through air, and Dev becomes obsessed with understanding sound waves, vibrations, and why his cousin Anjali's flute music is so beautiful.

slides.title: What is Sound?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Sound is a form of energy produced by vibrations. It travels as waves through a medium (air, water, or solid).

points.label: Speed of Sound
points.text: In air at 20°C: ~343 m/s. In water: ~1480 m/s. In steel: ~5960 m/s. Sound travels SLOWER than light.

points.label: Medium Required
points.text: Sound NEEDS a medium to travel. In a vacuum (no air), there is NO sound.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sound is made by vibrations and travels through air, water, or solid things.

slides.title: Sound Waves: Compressions and Rarefactions

points.label: What Happens
points.text: When something vibrates, it pushes and pulls the medium around it, creating compressions (crowded particles) and rarefactions (spread-out particles).

points.label: Wave Pattern
points.text: These compressions and rarefactions spread outward as a sound wave.

points.label: Visualization
points.text: Imagine throwing a stone in a pond—the ripples spread out. Sound waves are similar but in air, not water.

example.problem: Dev hits a drum. The drum skin vibrates 100 times per second. How many compressions are created in the air each second?
example.solution: Each vibration creates one compression and one rarefaction, so 100 vibrations = 100 compressions. This is the FREQUENCY of the sound: 100 Hz (Hz = cycles per second).

slides.inSimpleWords: Sound waves are made of squeezes and stretches in the air, spreading outward from the vibrating object.

slides.title: Frequency and Pitch

points.label: Frequency
points.text: How many vibrations happen per second, measured in Hertz (Hz).

points.label: Pitch
points.text: HIGH frequency = HIGH pitch (shrill sound like a whistle). LOW frequency = LOW pitch (deep sound like thunder).

points.label: Hearing Range
points.text: Humans can hear 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Babies hear higher frequencies; older people hear lower frequencies.

example.problem: Anjali plays a flute note at 440 Hz and a deeper note at 220 Hz. Which is higher in pitch?
example.solution: The 440 Hz note is higher pitch because higher frequency = higher pitch. This is actually the musical note 'A'!

slides.inSimpleWords: Fast vibrations = high pitch sounds. Slow vibrations = low pitch sounds.

slides.title: Loudness and Amplitude

points.label: Amplitude
points.text: How BIG the vibrations are. Larger vibrations = louder sound. Measured in decibels (dB).

points.label: Loudness Scale
points.text: 0 dB = silence. 30 dB = whisper. 60 dB = normal conversation. 80 dB = alarm clock. 110 dB = firecracker (harmful!). 130 dB = pain.

points.label: Indian Example
points.text: Diwali firecrackers (120-130 dB) can damage hearing if you don't wear earplugs. City traffic (80-90 dB) is louder than it should be.

slides.inSimpleWords: Big vibrations make loud sounds. Small vibrations make quiet sounds.

slides.title: Echo and Reflection of Sound

points.label: What is an Echo
points.text: Sound bounces off hard surfaces (walls, cliffs, buildings) and comes back to you.

points.label: Time Delay
points.text: The farther the surface, the longer the delay. Sound travels at ~343 m/s, so a 34-meter cliff = 0.1 second delay.

points.label: Soft Surfaces Absorb
points.text: Soft materials (carpets, curtains, foam) absorb sound and REDUCE echo. Hard surfaces (tiles, glass) REFLECT sound and CREATE echo.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sound bounces off hard surfaces and comes back—that's an echo.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Measuring Distance with Echo

example.problem: Dev shouts near a tall building and hears an echo after 2 seconds. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. How far away is the building?
example.solution: Sound travels to the building and back, so total distance = 2 × (distance to building). Total distance = 343 × 2 = 686 meters. Distance to building = 686 / 2 = 343 meters. (This is why echo delay depends on distance!)

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Silent Room
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari's house is next to a busy road, and Dev wants to create a quiet study room.

example.problem: The road noise is 80 dB. Dev plans to use soft curtains, carpets, and foam panels. Which materials will reduce sound the most?
example.solution: Heavy, soft materials (thick curtains, carpets, foam) absorb sound by converting vibrations to heat. Hard surfaces (glass, tile, plaster) reflect sound. Combination: foam panels on walls (absorb), thick curtains (absorb), carpets (absorb), no hard bare walls. Air gaps between panels add extra absorption. This is how recording studios work!

slides.inSimpleWords: Use soft, heavy materials to absorb sound and make a room quieter.

points.text: Sound is energy produced by vibrations, traveling as waves through air, water, or solids.
Sound needs a medium—it cannot travel in a vacuum.
Frequency = how many vibrations per second (Hz). High frequency = high pitch.
Amplitude = size of vibrations. Large vibrations = loud sound (decibels, dB).
Sound travels at ~343 m/s in air, much slower than light.
Hard surfaces reflect sound (creating echoes). Soft surfaces absorb sound (reducing noise).

subject: Science
title: Rohit's Science Fair: Electric Current and Chemistry
hook: Can electricity change the color of water? Can it create new substances? Discover electrochemistry.

characters.name: Swati
characters.role: Rohit's lab partner with excellent chemistry knowledge

slides.title: Chemical Effects of Electric Current
slides.storyContext: Rohit and Swati are preparing a science fair project when Dr. Patel challenges them to explore how electricity changes chemicals.

slides.title: The Electroplating Mystery
slides.storyContext: Rohit notices his kitchen tap is turning green (copper oxidation). Dr. Patel suggests that if electric current can RUST metals, maybe it can also PLATE metals (coat one metal with another). Rohit decides to electroplate a copper coin with silver for the science fair and discovers the hidden chemistry of electric current.

slides.title: What is Electrolysis?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Electrolysis is the breaking down of a chemical compound using electric current.

points.label: Requirements
points.text: You need: (1) a salt solution or molten salt, (2) two electrodes (positive and negative), (3) a power source (battery).

points.label: Example
points.text: Passing electricity through water (H₂O) breaks it into hydrogen gas (H₂) and oxygen gas (O₂).

slides.inSimpleWords: Electric current can split chemicals into new substances—this is called electrolysis.

slides.title: Electrodes: Anode and Cathode

points.label: Cathode
points.text: The NEGATIVE electrode (connected to the negative terminal of the battery). Attracts positive ions.

points.label: Anode
points.text: The POSITIVE electrode (connected to the positive terminal of the battery). Attracts negative ions.

points.label: Ion Movement
points.text: In a solution, positive ions (cations) move toward cathode; negative ions (anions) move toward anode.

example.problem: In a copper sulfate (CuSO₄) solution, what are the ions, and which electrode will they approach?
example.solution: Cu²⁺ (copper ions, positive) move to cathode. SO₄²⁻ (sulfate ions, negative) move to anode. This is how electroplating works!

slides.inSimpleWords: Positive ions go to the negative electrode; negative ions go to the positive electrode.

slides.title: Electrolysis of Water

points.label: The Reaction
points.text: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (water breaks into hydrogen and oxygen gases)

points.label: At the Cathode
points.text: Hydrogen gas (H₂) is produced—you see bubbles.

points.label: At the Anode
points.text: Oxygen gas (O₂) is produced—you see bubbles. Oxygen produced is about half the volume of hydrogen.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electric current breaks water into two gases: hydrogen and oxygen.

slides.title: Electroplating: Coating Metals

points.label: How It Works
points.text: The object to be plated (e.g., a copper coin) is placed at the cathode. A pure metal (e.g., silver) is placed at the anode. Current flows, and the anode metal dissolves and plates onto the cathode object.

points.label: The Reaction
points.text: Ag (silver at anode) → Ag⁺ (ions in solution) → Ag (coats the coin at cathode)

points.label: Real Applications
points.text: Jewelry making (gold plating), car parts (chrome plating), electronics (nickel plating).

example.problem: Rohit wants to coat a copper coin (cathode) with silver. He uses a silver electrode (anode) and a silver nitrate solution. What happens?
example.solution: Silver from the anode dissolves into Ag⁺ ions. These ions move to the cathode (copper coin) and gain electrons, becoming Ag metal. The coin gets a shiny silver coating!

slides.inSimpleWords: Electroplating uses electricity to coat one metal with another—this is how jewelry and shiny things are made.

slides.title: Electrochemical Refining: Purifying Metals

points.label: The Process
points.text: Impure copper is placed at the anode. Pure copper is placed at the cathode. Electric current causes pure copper to transfer to the cathode, leaving impurities behind.

points.label: Importance
points.text: Refining copper this way removes impurities like iron and zinc, producing 99.99% pure copper needed for electronics.

points.label: Indian Industry
points.text: India mines copper and refines it electrochemically for wiring, circuits, and industrial use.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electricity can purify metals by moving pure metal to one side and leaving dirt behind.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate

example.problem: Rohit electrolyzes a copper sulfate solution with copper electrodes. At the anode, copper dissolves: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. At the cathode, copper deposits: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. After 1 hour, 63.5 g of copper is deposited. How much copper dissolved at the anode?
example.solution: 63.5 g = 1 mole of Cu. For every mole of Cu deposited, 1 mole dissolves. So 63.5 g of copper dissolved at the anode. The solution stays balanced, but the copper redistributes from anode to cathode.

slides.title: Challenge: Clean and Restore Old Silver
slides.storyContext: Swati's grandmother has old silver jewelry that turned black (silver sulfide, Ag₂S). Dr. Patel suggests electrolysis can restore it.

example.problem: The tarnished silver (cathode) is placed in a solution with a pure silver anode. Electric current flows. Will the black tarnish disappear?
example.solution: At the cathode, silver ions from the solution plate onto the jewelry, covering the black tarnish. The anode (pure silver) dissolves, supplying fresh silver ions. The jewelry returns to shiny silver! This is called electrolytic cleaning.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electroplating can also clean and restore old metals by coating them with fresh, shiny metal.

points.text: Electrolysis is breaking down chemicals using electric current.
The cathode is negative; the anode is positive. Positive ions go to cathode; negative ions go to anode.
Electrolysis of water produces hydrogen gas at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode.
Electroplating coats one metal with another using electricity—used in jewelry, cars, and electronics.
Electrochemical refining purifies metals like copper to 99.99% purity.
The same process cleans tarnished jewelry by plating fresh metal over the black corrosion.

subject: Science
title: Isha's Monsoon Discovery: Lightning and Earthquakes
hook: What is lightning? How do earthquakes happen? Explore Earth's dramatic natural forces.

characters.name: Isha
characters.role: curious student in rural Odisha who experiences monsoons

characters.name: Teacher Malini
characters.role: science teacher who explains natural phenomena

slides.title: Some Natural Phenomena
slides.storyContext: During monsoon season in Odisha, Isha witnesses a spectacular thunderstorm with lightning and learns that earthquakes also happen in India.

slides.title: The Great Monsoon Storm
slides.storyContext: Isha watches a summer monsoon thunderstorm roll across her village. She sees lightning flash, hears thunder boom, and wonders how these things happen. Later, she learns about earthquakes when a minor tremor shakes her school. Teacher Malini and Raj help her understand these powerful natural phenomena.

slides.title: What Causes Lightning?

points.label: Build-up
points.text: During a storm, water droplets and ice crystals in clouds rub together, creating static electrical charge (like rubbing a balloon).

points.label: The Discharge
points.text: When the charge difference between cloud and ground becomes too large, electricity JUMPS—this is lightning. A lightning bolt is a giant spark!

points.label: Sequence
points.text: Lightning jumps from cloud to ground (or ground to cloud). Thunder is the sound from the hot air shocked by lightning.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity that jumps from clouds to the ground during storms.

slides.title: Thunder and Sound

points.label: What is Thunder
points.text: The lightning bolt heats the air around it to 30,000 K (5 times hotter than the sun's surface). Hot air EXPLODES, creating a shock wave = THUNDER.

points.label: Light vs. Sound
points.text: Light travels instantly (~300,000 km/s). Sound travels slowly (~343 m/s). So we see lightning first, then hear thunder later.

points.label: Measuring Distance
points.text: Count seconds between lightning and thunder, divide by 3 (roughly) to get distance in kilometers. E.g., 3 seconds = 1 km away.

example.problem: Isha sees lightning and counts 6 seconds before hearing thunder. How far away is the lightning strike?
example.solution: Distance = 6 seconds × 343 m/s = 2,058 meters ≈ 2 km. Or use the shortcut: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 km.

slides.inSimpleWords: We see lightning instantly but hear thunder later. Counting the delay tells us how far away the lightning is.

slides.title: Lightning Safety

points.label: Danger
points.text: Lightning strikes can kill or seriously injure. In India, ~2,000 deaths per year from lightning.

points.label: Safe Places
points.text: Inside a building or a car (metal protects you). Metal rods on buildings (lightning rods) safely direct electricity to the ground.

points.label: Unsafe Places
points.text: Under trees, in open fields, near metal objects, in water. Tall, conducting objects attract lightning.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stay inside during thunderstorms. Don't go under trees or into water.

slides.title: What Causes Earthquakes?

points.label: Earth's Layers
points.text: Earth has a crust (solid rock), mantle (hot rock), and core. The crust is broken into plates that slowly move.

points.label: Plate Tectonics
points.text: Plates collide, slide, or pull apart. When they get stuck and then suddenly slip, energy is RELEASED—this is an earthquake.

points.label: Seismic Waves
points.text: Earthquakes send waves through Earth's crust. P-waves (fast, push) and S-waves (slower, sideways) travel at different speeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's crust is made of moving plates. When they slip suddenly, the ground shakes—that's an earthquake.

slides.title: Earthquake Measurement: Richter Scale

points.label: The Scale
points.text: 1–3: Not felt. 4–5: Felt (minor damage). 6–7: Dangerous (serious damage). 8+: Catastrophic.

points.label: In India
points.text: The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake (9.1 magnitude) caused the tsunami that killed 230,000+ people. The 2001 Gujarat earthquake (7.7 magnitude) killed 20,000+.

points.label: Logarithmic
points.text: Each level is 32 times more powerful than the last. A 6 is NOT just slightly stronger than a 5; it's 32 times more powerful!

example.problem: The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake was magnitude 9.1. Compare it to a 7.1 earthquake.
example.solution: 9.1 - 7.1 = 2 levels. 2 levels × 32 per level = 32² = 1,024 times more powerful! That's why the 9.1 was catastrophic.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Richter scale measures earthquake strength. Each higher number means MUCH more power, not just a little more.

slides.title: Earthquake Safety and Preparation

points.label: Before
points.text: Know safe spots (under tables, against interior walls). Practice "drop, cover, and hold on."

points.label: During
points.text: DROP to hands and knees. COVER your head. HOLD ON to something sturdy. Stay away from windows and heavy objects.

points.label: After
points.text: Check for injuries. Get to open ground away from buildings. Listen to official warnings.

slides.inSimpleWords: If an earthquake happens: Drop, cover, and hold on. Get under a sturdy table or against an interior wall.

example.problem: P-waves travel at 6 km/s and S-waves at 3.5 km/s. An earthquake happens 100 km away. What is the time delay between when the P-wave and S-wave arrive at a seismometer?
example.solution: P-wave arrival time = 100 / 6 = 16.67 seconds. S-wave arrival time = 100 / 3.5 = 28.57 seconds. Time delay = 28.57 - 16.67 = 11.9 seconds ≈ 12 seconds. Scientists use this delay to locate earthquakes!

slides.title: Challenge: Build an Earthquake-Proof Building
slides.storyContext: After learning about earthquakes, Raj wants to design a school building that won't collapse in an earthquake.

example.problem: A building in Gujarat shakes during a 6.0 earthquake. Simple buildings with rigid walls crack and collapse. What design features would make it earthquake-proof?
example.solution: Use flexible materials (steel beams, flexible foundations). Wider base for stability. Shock absorbers and dampers to absorb shaking energy. Flexible connections so parts can move without breaking. Deep foundations in stable rock. Modern buildings in earthquake zones use these features—this is why new buildings survive earthquakes better than old ones.

slides.inSimpleWords: Buildings need to be flexible, not rigid, to survive earthquakes. They bend instead of breaking.

points.text: Lightning is a giant spark caused by electrical charge in storm clouds. We see it instantly, but hear the thunder (sound) later.
Thunder is the sound of air shocked by lightning—explosively hot and fast.
Count seconds between lightning and thunder to estimate distance (divide by 3 for rough km distance).
Earthquakes happen when Earth's crustal plates move and slip suddenly.
The Richter scale measures earthquake strength logarithmically—each level is ~32 times more powerful.
Safety: During lightning, stay inside. During earthquakes, drop, cover, and hold on.

subject: Science
title: Maya's Mirror Maze: Understanding Light and Reflection
hook: How do mirrors create images? Why do prisms make rainbows? Explore the secrets of light.

characters.name: Maya
characters.role: artist interested in how light works

characters.name: Aditya
characters.role: Maya's friend fascinated by light experiments

slides.title: Light
slides.storyContext: Maya builds a mirror maze for a school project and realizes she doesn't fully understand how mirrors work. Prof. Bhat offers to teach her.

slides.title: The Mirror Mystery
slides.storyContext: Maya is designing a mirror maze for her school fair when she realizes she can predict where light will go if she understands reflection. Prof. Bhat shows her that light travels in straight lines, bounces predictably off mirrors, and can be split into colors by a prism. Aditya joins in, and they build experiments to explore refraction, lenses, and the behavior of light.

slides.title: What is Light?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines and allows us to see.

points.label: Speed
points.text: Light travels at ~300,000 km/s in vacuum (and slightly slower in air or water).

points.label: Sources
points.text: The sun, light bulbs, candles, fire—anything hot enough glows. Objects don't glow themselves; we see them because they reflect light.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light is energy that travels very fast in straight lines. We see things because light reflects off them.

slides.title: Reflection: Laws of Reflection

points.label: Mirror Reflection
points.text: When light hits a smooth mirror, it bounces off. The angle of incidence (incoming) EQUALS the angle of reflection (bouncing).

points.label: Normal Line
points.text: An imaginary line perpendicular to the mirror surface. Angles are measured from this normal.

points.label: Real Application
points.text: This is why mirrors create images at the same angle as the object. Light traces a path you can predict mathematically.

example.problem: Light hits a mirror at 30° from the normal. At what angle does it reflect?
example.solution: Angle of incidence = 30°. By the law of reflection, angle of reflection = 30°. The light bounces off at the same angle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light bounces off a mirror at the same angle it comes in—like a ball bouncing off a wall.

slides.title: Images from Mirrors: Real and Virtual

points.label: Plane Mirror
points.text: A flat mirror (like at home). Creates a VIRTUAL image: same size, upright, same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

points.label: Curved Mirrors
points.text: Concave mirrors (curve inward) can create real, upside-down, magnified images. Convex mirrors (curve outward) create smaller images.

points.label: Periscope
points.text: Two mirrors at 45° angles allow you to see around corners—used in submarines and to peek over walls.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flat mirrors create images that look like the real thing but are reversed (mirror image). Curved mirrors can magnify or shrink.

slides.title: Refraction: Bending of Light

points.label: What Happens
points.text: When light passes from one medium (e.g., air) to another (e.g., water), it bends. The speed of light changes, so the direction changes.

points.label: Example
points.text: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent where it enters the water—the light bends as it exits the water.

points.label: Refractive Index
points.text: Each material has a refractive index. Water = 1.33, Glass = 1.5, Diamond = 2.42 (very high bending).

example.problem: Why does a swimming pool look shallower than it actually is?
example.solution: Light from the pool bottom bends as it exits the water into air. The light reaches your eye from a higher angle than it actually came from, so your brain thinks the light came from a shallower depth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light bends when it passes from one material to another, like air to water. This makes things look shifted or distorted.

slides.title: Prisms and Dispersion: Making Rainbows

points.label: White Light
points.text: Sunlight is white, but it's made of all colors mixed together (VIBGYOR: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red).

points.label: Different Speeds
points.text: Each color has a slightly different refractive index. Red light bends less; violet bends more.

points.label: Prism Separation
points.text: A glass prism bends different colors by different amounts, splitting white light into a rainbow.

slides.inSimpleWords: White light is made of all colors. A prism bends each color differently, separating them into a rainbow.

slides.title: Lenses: Convex and Concave

points.label: Convex Lenses
points.text: Bulge outward. Focus light to a point (converging). Used in magnifying glasses, cameras, and human eyes.

points.label: Concave Lenses
points.text: Curve inward. Spread light apart (diverging). Used in some eyeglasses for nearsightedness.

points.label: Focal Length
points.text: The distance from the lens where parallel light rays focus—a property of each lens.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convex lenses magnify and focus. Concave lenses spread light out. Together, they correct vision.

example.problem: Maya builds a pinhole camera—a box with a tiny hole and a screen. Light from a candle passes through the pinhole and forms an image on the screen. Why is the image upside down?
example.solution: Light travels in straight lines. Light from the top of the candle goes straight through the hole and hits the bottom of the screen. Light from the bottom goes through and hits the top. The image is inverted because light paths cross at the hole. This is how camera obscuras work—and similar to how human eyes work!

slides.title: Challenge: Design Glasses for Nearsightedness
slides.storyContext: Aditya is nearsighted and can only see clearly close up. Prof. Bhat challenges him to understand why concave lenses help.

example.problem: In nearsightedness, the eye focuses light TOO much, making distant objects blurry. A concave lens spreads light out BEFORE it reaches the eye. How does this help?
example.solution: The concave lens weakens the converging power of the eye, moving the focus point back onto the retina. Distant objects are now in focus. This is why people with myopia wear concave (diverging) lenses. Hyperopia (farsightedness) uses convex lenses instead.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nearsighted people need lenses that spread light out so the eye can focus on distant objects.

points.text: Light travels in straight lines at ~300,000 km/s and is the energy that lets us see.
Reflection: light bounces off mirrors at the same angle it comes in (angle of incidence = angle of reflection).
Plane mirrors create virtual images; curved mirrors can create real, magnified, or diminished images.
Refraction: light bends when passing between materials (like air to water) because its speed changes.
Prisms separate white light into colors because each color bends differently (dispersion).
Convex lenses focus light (magnifying glasses, cameras). Concave lenses spread light (correcting nearsightedness).
